questions.question: Which one of the following CPU scheduling algorithms cannot be preemptive?
questions.explanation:
Checking whether each scheduling algorithm supports preemption:

- SRTF is explicitly the preemptive version of Shortest-Job-First — it can preempt a running process whenever a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining time.
- Round Robin is inherently preemptive — it forcibly preempts a running process once its time quantum expires.
- Priority Scheduling can be implemented in either a preemptive form (a higher-priority arrival preempts the current process) or non-preemptive form — so it certainly can be preemptive.
- FCFS (First Come First Serve) is defined by running processes strictly to completion in arrival order — there is no mechanism within FCFS for a later-arriving process to interrupt/preempt the one currently executing. It is inherently non-preemptive by definition.

Answer: First Come First Serve (FCFS) Scheduling cannot be preemptive.

questions.question:
Which of the following tasks is/are the responsibility/responsibilities of the memory
management unit (MMU) in a system with paging-based memory management?

options.A: Allocate a new page table for a newly created process
options.B: Translate a virtual address to a physical address using the page table
options.C: Raise a trap when a virtual address is not found in the page table
options.D: Raise a trap when a process tries to write to a page marked with read-only permission in the page table

questions.explanation:
The MMU is hardware that sits between CPU and memory. Its jobs:
- Translate virtual address [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] physical address using the page table True
- Raise a trap (page fault) when the entry is invalid / not present True
- Raise a trap when a write is attempted on a read-only page True

Allocating a page table for a new process is done by the OS (software), not the MMU.

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

questions.question: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?

options.A: The TLB performs an associative search in parallel on all its valid entries using page number of incoming virtual address.
options.B: If the virtual address of a word given by CPU has a TLB hit, but the subsequent search for the word results in a cache miss, then the word will always be present in the main memory.
options.C: The memory access time using a given inverted page table is always same for all incoming virtual addresses.
options.D: In a system that uses hashed page tables, if two distinct virtual addresses V1 and V2 map to the same value while hashing, then the memory access time of these addresses will not be the same.

questions.explanation:
Check each statement (we need the FALSE one):
- The TLB is associative memory and compares all entries in parallel [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- A TLB hit means the page is in main memory, so on a cache miss the word is surely in main memory [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Inverted page table: the frame is found by searching (or hashing and following a chain), so the time depends on the address [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- In a hashed page table, colliding addresses sit on the same chain at different positions, so their access times differ [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Option 3 is FALSE

questions.question:
A system has a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) that has a reach of [latex]1[/latex] MB. TLB reach is defined as the total amount of physical memory that can be accessed through the TLB entries. The paging system uses pages of size [latex]4[/latex] KB. The virtual address space is [latex]64[/latex] GB and physical address space is [latex]1[/latex] GB. If each TLB entry stores a [latex]4[/latex]-bit process id, page number, frame number, and a [latex]2[/latex]-bit control field, then the size of the TLB (in bytes) is ________. (answer in integer)
Note: [latex]1 {K}=2^{10}, 1 {M}=2^{20}, 1 {G}=2^{30}[/latex]
questions.explanation:
TLB reach [latex]=[/latex] page size [latex]\times[/latex] number of TLB entries, so number of entries [latex]=\dfrac{1\text{ MB}}{4\text{ KB}}=\dfrac{2^{20}}{2^{12}}=2^8=256[/latex] entries.

Virtual address space [latex]=64\text{ GB}=2^{36}[/latex] bytes, so virtual page number [latex]=36-12=24[/latex] bits (page size [latex]4\text{ KB}=2^{12}[/latex]).
Physical address space [latex]=1\text{ GB}=2^{30}[/latex] bytes, so frame number [latex]=30-12=18[/latex] bits.

Each TLB entry stores: [latex]4[/latex]-bit PID [latex]+[/latex] [latex]24[/latex]-bit page number [latex]+[/latex] [latex]18[/latex]-bit frame number [latex]+[/latex] [latex]2[/latex]-bit control [latex]=4+24+18+2=48[/latex] bits [latex]=6[/latex] bytes per entry.

Total TLB size [latex]=256\times6=1536[/latex] bytes.

Answer: 1536

questions.question:
A computer has two processors, [latex]M_1[/latex] and [latex]M_2[/latex]. Four processes [latex]P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4[/latex] with CPU bursts of 20, 16, 25, and 10 milliseconds, respectively, arrive at the same time and these are the only processes in the system. The scheduler uses non-preemptive priority scheduling, with priorities decided as follows:

[latex]M_1[/latex] uses priority of execution for the processes as, [latex]P_1 > P_3 > P_2 > P_4[/latex], i.e., [latex]P_1[/latex] and [latex]P_4[/latex] have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.
[latex]M_2[/latex] uses priority of execution for the processes as, [latex]P_2 > P_3 > P_4 > P_1[/latex], i.e., [latex]P_2[/latex] and [latex]P_1[/latex] have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.

A process [latex]P_i[/latex] is scheduled to a processor [latex]M_k[/latex], if the processor is free and no other process [latex]P_j[/latex] is waiting with higher priority. At any given point of time, a process can be allocated to any one of the free processors without violating the execution priority rules. Ignore the context switch time. What will be the average waiting time of the processes in milliseconds?
questions.explanation:
All four processes arrive together at [latex]t=0[/latex] with two free processors, so two of them start immediately. Since [latex]P_1[/latex] is [latex]M_1[/latex]'s top priority and [latex]P_2[/latex] is [latex]M_2[/latex]'s top priority (and conveniently each is the other machine's lowest priority, so there's no conflict), the natural non-conflicting start is [latex]P_1\to M_1[/latex] and [latex]P_2\to M_2[/latex], both beginning at [latex]t=0[/latex].

[latex]P_2[/latex] (burst [latex]16[/latex]) finishes first, at [latex]t=16[/latex], freeing [latex]M_2[/latex]. Among the still-waiting [latex]P_3,P_4[/latex], [latex]M_2[/latex]'s priority order ([latex]P_2{>}P_3{>}P_4{>}P_1[/latex]) favors [latex]P_3[/latex], so [latex]P_3[/latex] starts on [latex]M_2[/latex] at [latex]t=16[/latex], running until [latex]16+25=41[/latex].

[latex]P_1[/latex] (burst [latex]20[/latex]) finishes next, at [latex]t=20[/latex], freeing [latex]M_1[/latex]. Only [latex]P_4[/latex] remains waiting, so it starts on [latex]M_1[/latex] at [latex]t=20[/latex], running until [latex]20+10=30[/latex].

Waiting times: [latex]P_1{:}\,0[/latex], [latex]P_2{:}\,0[/latex], [latex]P_3{:}\,16-0=16[/latex], [latex]P_4{:}\,20-0=20[/latex].

Average [latex]=\dfrac{0+0+16+20}{4}=\dfrac{36}{4}=9[/latex].

Answer: 9

questions.question:
A multithreaded program P executes with x number of threads and uses y number of locks for
ensuring mutual exclusion while operating on shared memory locations. All locks in the
program are non-reentrant, i.e., if a thread holds a lock l, then it cannot re-acquire lock l
without releasing it. If a thread is unable to acquire a lock, it blocks until the lock becomes
available. The minimum value of x and the minimum value of y together for which execution
of P can result in a deadlock are:
questions.explanation:
The locks are non-reentrant: if a single thread holding lock l tries to acquire l again, it blocks forever waiting for itself. So one thread and one lock are enough.

Answer: x = 1, y = 1

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

Semaphore [latex]A[/latex] (init [latex]1[/latex]) acts as a mutex guarding the critical section (print "*", increment [latex]X[/latex], and the [latex]X{=}{=}2[/latex] check), so all three processes enter this section one at a time, and exactly one of them (whichever happens to be the second to enter) will see [latex]X{=}{=}2[/latex] and print "[latex]\$[/latex]" then signal [latex]B[/latex]. Since the third process cannot even attempt this section until the second has released [latex]A[/latex] (which only happens after printing "[latex]\$[/latex]"), the global order is forced to always be: [latex]{*},{*},\$,{*}[/latex] — exactly two stars, then the dollar, then the third star. A pattern like [latex]{*}{*}{*}\$[/latex] (three stars before the dollar) can never occur.

After the dollar, semaphore [latex]B[/latex] gets exactly one initial permit, which starts a chain: each process that consumes the permit via [latex]\text{Wait}(B)[/latex] prints "[latex]\#[/latex]" and immediately regenerates the next permit via its own [latex]\text{Signal}(B)[/latex], letting the next process through in turn. The remaining ("third") star can interleave with this "[latex]\#[/latex]" chain at any point before that third process itself joins the chain — i.e. before any [latex]\#[/latex], after exactly one [latex]\#[/latex], or after exactly two [latex]\#[/latex]'s (but never after all three, since the third process must complete its own star/critical-section before it can take part in the [latex]\#[/latex] chain at all).

Answer: **$*###, **$#*##, and **$##*# are all possible; ***$### is impossible.

questions.question:
Consider the following four processes with arrival times (in milliseconds) and their length of CPU burst (in milliseconds) as shown below:
These processes are run on a single processor using preemptive Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling algorithm. If the average waiting time of the processes is 1 millisecond, then the value of Z is __________.
questions.explanation:
Average waiting time 1 ms [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] total waiting time = 4 ms.

SRTF up to t = 4: P1 runs 0-1; P2 (burst 1) preempts and runs 1-2; P1 runs 2-4 and finishes. P1 waited 1, P2 waited 0.

At t = 4, P3 (3 ms, arrived at 3) and P4 (Z) are left. For the total to be 4, they must wait 3 in total.
With Z = 2: P4 runs 4-6 (wait 0), P3 runs 6-9 (wait 9 [latex]-[/latex] 3 [latex]-[/latex] 3 = 3). Total = 1 + 0 + 3 + 0 = 4 True

Answer: 2

questions.question:
Consider the following proposed solution for the critical section problem. There are n processes: [latex]P_{0}...P_{n-1}[/latex] . In the code,function [latex]pmax[/latex] returns an integer not smaller than any of its arguments. For all i, t[i] is initialized to zero.

Which one of the following is TRUE about the above solution?

options.A: At most one process can be in the critical section at any time
options.B: The bounded wait condition is satisfied

questions.explanation:
This is a bakery-style algorithm: a process enters only after every other process with a smaller (non-zero) ticket has finished, so mutual exclusion holds.

But two processes can pick the same ticket (pmax is not atomic). Then each waits for the other (t[j] [latex]\le[/latex] t[i] holds both ways) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] deadlock, so progress and bounded waiting also fail.

Answer: At most one process can be in the critical section at any time
